hero.title: Language syntax, types, and coercion rules.
hero.description: J++ is a strictly typed language with two primitives: number and string. There is no implicit coercion—mixed-type mistakes are rejected at compile time.

sections.title: Language overview
sections.summary: J++ compiles to JavaScript but rejects JavaScript-style implicit coercion. Arithmetic and text operations stay predictable.

sections.title: Syntax and keywords
sections.summary: Declare with ye, print with bol, branch with agar/nahi, and loop with jabtak or ke liye … tak.

sections.title: Types and coercion
sections.summary: Types are inferred from the first assignment. Reassignment and operators must match those types exactly.

principles.title: No implicit coercion
principles.text: J++ never silently converts between number and string. Invalid mixes fail at compile time.

principles.title: Deterministic text
principles.text: . concatenates strings only—it is not overloaded for numbers.

principles.title: Stable variable types
principles.text: A variable keeps the type from its first ye assignment; later values must match.

syntaxExample:
ye a = 5
ye b = 10
ye total = a + b
bol total

ye first = "hello"
ye second = "world"
bol first . " " . second
operatorRows: number or string (same type both sides)

keywordGroups.title: Core statements
items: Declare a variable; type is inferred from the first assignment.

keywordGroups.title: Loops and control
items: While loop while the condition is true.
Exclusive upper bound in a for loop.

precedence: Primary expressions: literals, identifiers, and parenthesized values.

typeCoercion.summary: J++ has no implicit type coercion. Unlike JavaScript, expressions like 5 + "hi" or "3" + 4 are compile errors, not silent conversions.

rules.title: Two primitive types
rules.text: Only number and string exist. Types are inferred from literals (5, 3.14, "text") on declaration.

rules.title: Assignment must match
rules.text: After ye x = 5, assigning a string to x fails: "Type mismatch: cannot assign string to x (declared as number)".

rules.title: Operators are type-locked
rules.text: + - * / require both operands to be number. . requires both operands to be string.

rules.title: No string–number mixing
rules.text: You cannot use + to concatenate strings or . to join numbers. Pick the operator that matches the types.

rules.title: Comparisons need consistent types
rules.text: Compare numbers to numbers and strings to strings. Mixed-type comparisons are rejected.

typeCoercion.validExample:
ye count = 2
ye label = "items"
ye next = count + 1
ye msg = label . ": " . "ready"
bol msg
typeCoercion.invalidExample:
ye x = 5
x = "wrong"

ye a = 1
ye b = "2"
ye bad = a + b

ye s = "hi"
ye also = s + 1

documents.title: J++ Language
documents.text: J++ is a small strictly typed language that compiles to JavaScript. It removes JavaScript-style implicit coercion. Design goals: deterministic arithmetic (+ - * / on numbers only), deterministic text (. on strings only), compile-time type feedback, and stable variable types from first assignment.

documents.title: Syntax and keywords
documents.text: Keywords: ye (declare), bol (print), agar (if), nahi (else), nahi agar (else-if), jabtak (while), ke liye (for), tak (for bound), break, continue. Operators: + - * / numeric only; . string concat only; == != < > <= >= for comparisons. Precedence: primary, then * /, then ., then + -, then comparisons.

documents.title: Types and coercion
documents.text: Primitive types: number and string, inferred on ye. No implicit coercion. Assignment to an existing variable must match its declared type. + - * / require number operands. . requires string operands. Cannot assign string to a number variable or vice versa. Examples of errors: number + string, string + number, reassigning ye x = 5 with a string.
